title: Check against the proven cases
question: Do the firms and professionals named in the building-inspection and Public Works cases, or on the extra-scrutiny list, stand out on these measures in the years the conduct covered?
finding: The speed test does not pick out the proven cases. Of 8 people and firms from the case files and the extra-scrutiny list with enough permits to test, 0 meet the test for consistently faster in the years the conduct covered. Rodrigo Santos (2012–2019): faster on 51% of 1,307 jobs, not distinguishable from like permits. SIA Consulting (2012–2021): faster on 42% of 347 jobs, somewhat slower: beyond the usual threshold only. 1 favourable result on another measure: SIA Consulting's full-review applications reached issue 83% of the time against 71% for like applications, enough to be listed in the screen 'Always approved, never held'. 1 result runs the other way: Harold Howell (Mercury Engineering Group, Inc.) is consistently slower on building permits (faster than like permits on only 36% of jobs). A method that cannot see the cases the courts have already proven cannot be read as clearing anyone it does not flag.
how: The names are taken from the case files (the engineer and the design firm in the building-inspection case; the contractors in the Public Works case) and from Building Inspection's published extra-scrutiny list. Their permits are every building permit whose contact rows carry the person's name or the firm's name as the case file or the list gives it. The years are read from each case file's own timeline: from the first dated payment or gift to the last year those entries mention; for a listed person, every year up to the listing, with the years after it shown separately. The same like-for-like measures are then computed on those permits alone, with the same cuts as the screens above.
limits: The proven conduct was about particular inspections, particular plan checks and money diverted from clients, none of which needs to show up as a faster average permit: a paid-for sign-off can change one job without moving an average, and a plan can be approved that should not be without being approved any sooner. A person is matched on the name typed on the permit, which can catch a namesake and miss a misspelling; each match here also carries the firm or the professional role the source gives. Days to issue is the only clock in the published data; who inspected what, and with what result, is not published at all. Being on the extra-scrutiny list or in a case file says nothing about any permit listed here.
